steps.title: Comparatives and superlatives
steps.html:
AdjectiveComparativeSuperlative
short: quietquieter thanthe quietest
ending in -y: lazylazier thanthe laziest
long: creativemore creative thanthe most creative
goodbetter thanthe best
badworse thanthe worst
farfurther thanthe furthest
the sameas useful as—

One-syllable adjectives add -er / -est: quiet → quieter → the quietest. Double a final consonant after one vowel: big → bigger.

Adjectives of two or more syllables use more / the most: more careful, the most creative. Two-syllable words ending in -y take -ier: lazy → lazier.

than after a comparative; the before a superlative. She is quieter than me. He is the most useful person here.

Make the difference bigger or smaller with much or a bit: much quieter, a bit more careful.

You compared amounts in Lesson 14 (more than my electricity bill). This lesson compares qualities.

options: people who prefer to listen rather than talk
steps.answer: people who prefer to listen rather than talk

steps.title: The quiet ones
steps.html:
Some people love a big group. They talk to everyone, they share their ideas quickly, and they feel happy when the room is looking at them. We call these people extroverts. Other people are different. They think first and speak later, they prefer a small group or an empty room, and they often do their best work alone. These are introverts — the quiet ones.

For a long time, most schools and most companies wanted the first type. A confident, sociable student got more attention than a shy one. In many offices the loudest voice in the meeting was also the most powerful voice. But is that fair?

The writer Susan Cain says no. Her best-selling book Quiet argues that introverts are just as creative and just as hard-working as extroverts. They are usually more patient, too, and they are often better listeners. Their ideas are not louder. They are simply slower — and sometimes they are the strongest ideas in the room.

Cain says something more surprising as well: a team of only extroverts is not the best team. A good team needs both. The talkers move a project forward; the quiet ones notice the problem nobody mentioned.

Of course, nobody is one hundred per cent one type. Most of us are a bit of both, and we change with the situation. The important thing is not to become somebody else. If you are the quietest person in your class, that is not a weakness. It is a different kind of strength.

Sources. Written for this course. The argument it summarises — that introverts are undervalued in schools and offices, and that mixed teams work better — is from Susan Cain, Quiet (2012). No wording is taken from the book.
